etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English utter, from out (adjective) and Old English ūtera, comparative of ūt (“out”). Compare outer.

quote.citation: 1708, Francis Atterbury, Fourteen Sermons Preach'd on Several Occasions, Preface:
quote.text: They  […]  are utter strangers to all those anxious  […] thoughts which  […] disquiet mankind.

quote.citation: 1920, Edgar Rice Burroughs, Thuvia, Maiden of Mars‎[1], HTML edition, The Gutenberg Project, published 2008:
quote.text: His eyes could not penetrate the darkness even to the distinguishing of his hand before his face, while the banths, he knew, could see quite well, though absence of light were utter.

definitions.definition: (now poetic, literary) Outer; furthest out, most remote: outmost. [from 10th c.]

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English utter, partly from utter (adjective, adverb), partly from Middle Dutch uteren.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To produce (speech or other sounds) with one's voice.

quote.citation: 1560, [William Whittingham et al., transl.], The Bible and Holy Scriptures Conteyned in the Olde and Newe Testament. […] (the Geneva Bible), Geneva:  […]  Rouland Hall, →OCLC, Prouerbes I:20, folio 267, verso:
quote.text: Wiſdome cryeth without: ſhe vttereth her voyce in the ſtretes.

quote.citation: 1748, Tobias Smollett, chapter 50, in The Adventures of Roderick Random‎[2], volume 2, London: J. Osborn, page 156:
quote.text: [H]e made no other reply, for some time, than lifting up his eyes, clasping his hands, and uttering a hollow groan.

quote.citation: 1868, Louisa M[ay] Alcott, chapter 17, in Little Women: […], part first, Boston, Mass.: Roberts Brothers, published 1869, →OCLC, page 263:
quote.text: […]  Laurie slyly pulled the parrot’s tail, which caused Polly to utter an astonished croak,  […]

quote.citation: 1997, Don DeLillo, Underworld: A Novel, New York, N.Y.: Scribner Classics, →ISBN, page 543:
quote.text: I wanted to look up velleity and quotidian and memorize the fuckers for all time, spell them, learn them, pronounce them syllable by syllable—vocalize, phonate, utter the sounds, say the words for all they're worth.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To reveal or express (an idea, thought, desire, etc.) with speech.

quote.citation: 1644, John Milton, Areopagitica; a Speech of Mr. John Milton for the Liberty of Unlicenc’d Printing, to the Parlament of England, London: [s.n.], →OCLC, page 35:
quote.text: Give me the liberty to know, to utter, and to argue freely according to conſcience, above all liberties.

quote.citation: 1749, Henry Fielding, “The Trial of Partridge, the Schoolmaster, for Incontinency; The Evidence of his Wife; A short Reflection on the Wisdom of our Law; with other grave Matters, which those will like best who understand them most”, in The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling, volume I, London: A[ndrew] Millar, […], →OCLC, book II, page 118:
quote.text: […]  tho’ a few odd Fellows will utter their own Sentiments in all Places, yet much the greater Part of Mankind have enough of the Courtier to accommodate their Converſation to the Taſte and Inclination of their Superiors.

quote.citation: 1871–1872, George Eliot [pseudonym; Mary Ann Evans], chapter LXXXIII, in Middlemarch […], volume IV, Edinburgh, London: William Blackwood and Sons, →OCLC, book VIII, page 323:
quote.text: Each had been full of thoughts which neither of them could begin to utter.

quote.citation: 1959, Muriel Spark, “Memento Mori”, in Time‎[3], New York, N.Y., published 1964, page 213:
quote.text: “Your master,” he declared, “has uttered a damnable lie about a dead friend of mine.”

quote.citation: 1995, Rohinton Mistry, A Fine Balance, Toronto, Ont.: McClelland and Stewart, part 11, page 528:
quote.text: “Don’t worry about me,” he uttered with minimum lip movement.

definitions.definition: (transitive, figurative) To produce (a noise) (of an inanimate object).
(transitive, obsolete) To spit or blow (something) out of one's mouth.

quote.text: He looked in vain for the sage Nicholas Vedder, with his broad face, double chin, and fair long pipe, uttering clouds of tobacco smoke instead of idle speeches;  […]

quote.citation: 1821 September, Charles Lamb, “The Old Benchers of the Inner Temple”, in The London Magazine, volume 4, number 21, page 280:
quote.text: Four little winged marble boys used to play their virgin fancies, spouting out ever fresh streams from their innocent-wanton lips, in the square of Lincoln’s-inn  […]  Are the stiff-wigged living figures, that still flitter and chatter about that area, less gothic in appearance? or, is the splutter of their hot rhetoric one half so refreshing and innocent, as the little cool playful streams those exploded cherubs uttered?

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To emit or give off (breath).

definitions.definition: (transitive, archaic) To shed (a tear or tears).

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To offer (something) for sale; to sell.

quote.citation: 1735, Jonathan Swift, Drapier’s Letters, Letter 3, in The Works of Jonathan Swift, Dublin: George Faulkner, Volume 4, p. 123,[6]
quote.text: There is nothing remaining to preserve us from Ruin, but that the whole Kingdom should continue in a firm determinate Resolution never to receive or utter this FATAL Coin:

quote.citation: 1842, cited in Supplement to The Jurist, containing a Digest of All the Reported Cases  […]  published during the year 1842, p. 49,[7]
quote.text: If two persons jointly prepare counterfeit coin, and then utter it in different shops, apart from each other, but in concert, and intending to share the proceeds, the utterings of each are the joint utterings of both, and they may be convicted jointly.

quote.citation: 1914, Section 87G(2), Crimes Act 1914 (Cth)
quote.text: A person shall not utter a postage stamp knowing it to be forged.

quote.citation: 1948, 18 U.S. Code § 486, Uttering coins of gold, silver or other metal
quote.text: Whoever, except as authorized by law, makes or utters or passes, or attempts to utter or pass, any coins of gold or silver or other metal, or alloys of metals, intended for use as current money, whether in the resemblance of coins of the United States or of foreign countries, or of original design, shall be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than five years, or both.

quote.citation: 1875, George Hayter Chubb, Protection from fire and thieves including the construction of locks, safes, strong-rooms, and fireproof buildings : burglary, and the means of preventing it; fire, its detection, prevention, and extinction; etc. : also a complete list of patents for locks and safes‎[9], page 23:
